concepts.title: Light Field Cameras
concepts.one_liner: Light field cameras use an array of tiny lenses to capture a scene from hundreds of different viewing angles, similar to how raindrops refract panoramas.
concepts.content: When it rains, every raindrop refracts a panorama of the scene around it. What you are seeing is not just one photo but hundreds of images of the scene, one in each raindrop, all from slightly different angles. Specially designed cameras called light field cameras have been made that do the same thing. These cameras use an array of tiny lenses rather than raindrops to capture what the scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles. From that density of information, they can achieve many interesting tricks, such as triangulating the depth of objects in the scene and synthetically refocusing the image after it has been taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard cameras collapse light into a single 2D projection, losing directional information. Light field cameras solve this by capturing the 'light field'—the direction and intensity of light rays—allowing for post-capture adjustments like refocusing and depth estimation.
concepts.recap_md: - Light field cameras use micro-lens arrays to capture a scene from multiple simultaneous angles.

concepts.title: Plato's Cave Metaphor for Vision
concepts.one_liner: An image is a crude projection of reality that collapses 3D geometry into a 2D grid, much like the shadows in Plato's Allegory of the Cave.
concepts.content: In the Allegory of the Cave, Plato imagined a group of prisoners chained up in a cave whose only experience of the outside world is through shadows cast on the cave's wall. When we look at images, we think we are directly seeing reality, but the situation is actually much more like Plato's cave. An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state. It collapses all the 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid of pixels. From any given viewing angle, most of the scene is occluded. Materials are only depicted in terms of how photons bounce off their surfaces; what's below the surface may be completely omitted. When you look at a picture, there is more you don't see than you do. One job of a vision system is to infer everything you can't see given everything you can.
concepts.motivation_md: This metaphor highlights the fundamental challenge of computer vision: reconstructing a complex, 3D world from incomplete, 2D projections that omit significant physical information.
concepts.recap_md: - Images are 2D projections that collapse 3D geometry and occlude much of the physical scene.

concepts.title: Visual Cues for Wetness

position.section_title: How Do You Know Something Is Wet?

concepts.one_liner: The human visual system can recognize material properties like wetness without physical contact by interpreting visual cues such as changes in darkness and reflectance.
concepts.content: Our visual system allows us to recognize not just objects, but also material. We can tell if something will feel hot or cold, soft or hard, smooth or rugged. We can also recognize if something is wet or not without touching it. For example, sand looks darker when it's wet. This raises interesting questions for vision: Does everything wet look darker than when it is dry? How can we tell which parts of a surface are dark because they are wet and which ones are dark because they are under a shadow?
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how materials change appearance under different physical states (like wetness) is crucial for computer vision systems to accurately interpret surface properties and lighting conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual systems identify material states like wetness through indirect cues like surface darkness.

concepts.title: Tree shadows and image formation
concepts.one_liner: The small openings between tree leaves act as pinhole cameras, projecting circular images of the sun onto the ground.
concepts.content: When walking under the shadow of a tree on a bright sunny day, light rays pass through the holes between leaves, creating spots on the floor. While one might expect these spots to have irregular shapes matching the openings, they appear circular and of similar size. This phenomenon occurs because the spacing between the leaves forms pinhole cameras. These tiny holes project copies of the sun onto the floor; when the openings are small enough, the shape of the projected light is dominated by the shape of the sun rather than the shape of the opening. This is clearly demonstrated during a solar eclipse, where the shadow of a tree contains many crescent-shaped copies of the sun.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains a common but often overlooked optical phenomenon, illustrating how simple apertures in nature can function as imaging systems (pinhole cameras) that project the shape of a light source.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaps between tree leaves act as natural pinhole cameras.
 - The circular spots seen in tree shadows are actually projected images of the sun.
 - During an eclipse, these spots change shape to match the sun's crescent profile.

When the openings between leaves are small enough, the shape of the projected spot light is dominated by the shape of the sun.

concepts.title: Pinhole camera
concepts.one_liner: A pinhole camera is an optical system where a small aperture projects an image of a light source onto a surface.
concepts.content: Pinhole cameras can be formed by the spacing between the leaves of a tree. The tiny holes between the leaves create a multitude of pinholes that project different copies of the sun on the floor. When the openings between leaves are small enough, the shape of the projected spot light is dominated by the shape of the sun rather than the shape of the aperture itself.
concepts.motivation_md: Pinhole cameras represent the simplest form of image formation, demonstrating how light traveling in straight lines through a small point can create a coherent image without lenses.
concepts.recap_md:
- Small apertures project the shape of the light source onto a surface.
 - The resulting image shape is dominated by the source (e.g., the sun) if the hole is small enough.
 - Natural examples include gaps between leaves in a tree canopy.

concepts.title: Perceiving horizontal and vertical surfaces
concepts.one_liner: The perception of a surface as horizontal or vertical is driven by the orientation of vanishing points and the resulting horizon line.
concepts.content: The perception of surface orientation, such as distinguishing between a floor and a wall, depends on the arrangement of vanishing points—the points where parallel lines appear to intersect. In a drawing of a horizontal surface, vanishing points are typically located above the drawing, compatible with a horizontal horizon line. Conversely, if a vanishing point is located below the figure, it can give the impression of looking at a vertical wall from a high camera angle. The horizon line of the plane, which connects the vanishing points, appears horizontal for ground surfaces and vertical for certain wall orientations, significantly altering how the viewer perceives the scene's geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how we perceive orientation helps explain how the human visual system and computer vision algorithms reconstruct 3D geometry from 2D images using perspective cues.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points are the locations where parallel lines appear to intersect in a 2D projection.
 - A horizontal horizon line connecting vanishing points suggests a horizontal surface like a floor.
 - The relative position of vanishing points determines whether a surface is perceived as vertical or horizontal.

However, on the drawing on the right, one of the vanishing points is below the figure and gives the impression that the camera is looking at a vertical wall (the camera seems to be higher than the visible part of the wall). concepts.title: Vanishing points
concepts.one_liner: Vanishing points are the points in a perspective drawing or image where parallel lines appear to intersect.
concepts.content: Vanishing points are the points in which parallel lines intersect in a projection. The arrangement of these points defines the horizon line of a plane (the line that connects both vanishing points). The position of these points relative to the image frame—whether they are above, below, or to the side—determines the perceived orientation of surfaces and the camera's viewpoint relative to those surfaces.
concepts.motivation_md: Vanishing points are fundamental to perspective projection, allowing 3D depth and orientation to be encoded into and recovered from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points are where parallel lines meet in perspective.
 - The line connecting two vanishing points on a plane forms that plane's horizon line.
 - Their location informs the viewer about the camera's orientation and height.

concepts.title: Understanding motion blur
concepts.one_liner: Motion blur occurs when a camera sensor collects light while moving, resulting in an average of translated image copies.
concepts.content: When taking a picture from a moving vehicle, images often appear blurry because the camera sensor collects light over a period of time while the car is in motion. The resulting picture is the average of several translated copies of the same image. Notably, the amount of blur is not uniform for all objects; things that are far away may remain sharp, while nearby objects appear very blurry. This blur is determined by the car's speed, the camera's exposure time, and the distance between the camera and the objects in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion blur is a critical concept in both photography and computer vision, as it provides cues about the relative depth of objects and the velocity of the observer.
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion blur is the temporal average of translated images during sensor exposure.
 - Nearby objects experience more motion blur than distant objects.
 - Blur intensity depends on speed, exposure time, and object distance.

key_passage.text: Blur is due to the fact that the camera sensor is collecting light during a period of time while the car is moving and the picture that results is the average of several translated copies of the same image.

concepts.title: Accidents and the principle of continuity
concepts.one_liner: The principle of continuity suggests that smooth, continuous line segments likely belong to a single object rather than being a coincidental alignment.
concepts.content:
The principle of continuity, a concept from Gestalt psychology, posits that if you see smooth, continuous line segments, you assume they lie on a single object. This is based on the idea that it would be a significant coincidence for the contours of two separate objects to perfectly align. While the generic view principle suggests we should avoid interpreting scenes based on such "accidents," real photographs often contain coincidences due to the sheer complexity and number of elements they contain. For example, in Dorothea Lange's "Migrant Mother," one can find instances where a finger boundary aligns with a lip contour or creases on two different shirts align perfectly. Rule-based vision algorithms often fail when they do not account for these exceptions to the principle of continuity.

[FIGURE:2962e76f5808a7be]

Despite this, other groupings are also possible.

[FIGURE:d7efe27713f24942]
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the tension between perceptual rules (like Gestalt principles) and the reality of visual 'accidents' or coincidences, which is vital for building robust computer vision systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- The principle of continuity assumes continuous lines belong to the same object.
 - 'Accidents' occur when unrelated object contours coincidentally align from a specific viewpoint.
 - Vision algorithms must handle these coincidences to avoid errors in object segmentation.

concepts.title: Cues for Support
concepts.one_liner: The relative location of an object and its shadow serves as a powerful visual cue for determining physical contact and support.
concepts.content: Determining whether one object supports another often relies on specific visual cues. The relative location between an object and its shadow on the ground is a powerful cue for contact; for instance, a drop shadow can indicate that a ball is hovering above a surface, while a slack string or the specific placement of a shadow can provide evidence that the ball is in contact with the surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying support relationships is essential for understanding the physical structure and stability of a 3D scene from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Shadows provide strong cues about the distance between an object and a surface.
 - Contact is perceived when the object and its shadow meet.
 - Other physical cues, like strings or points of contact, help confirm support relationships.

concepts.title: The role of context in pixel recognition
concepts.one_liner: The recognition of individual pixels or small image patches depends heavily on the surrounding context and the whole image rather than just local intensity values.
concepts.content: The minimum number of pixels needed to form a recognizable image depends on the image, and it is possible to create recognizable images with very few pixels. When examining a single pixel—such as a dark gray pixel at row 13 and column 12—it is often impossible to identify its meaning in isolation. For example, a pen might be barely three pixels long and one pixel wide. Recognition of such a pixel cannot come solely from its intensity or the few pixels nearby, as many different world objects could map to similar intensities. Instead, the whole image and the context of the pen provide the necessary information for recognition. Taken in isolation, those pixels are impossible to recognize. Here we show, from left to right, the hand, the blue mug, and the pen. ![Small image patches from in isolation. It is difficult to recognize image patches outside their natural context.](figures/visionscience/dalle-small.png){#fig-small-dalle}
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the role of context explains why local features are often ambiguous and why global scene information is crucial for accurate object identification in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Individual pixels or small patches are often impossible to recognize in isolation.

concepts.title: Vision as a dynamical system

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: Vision acts as a dynamical system where prolonged observation reveals increasing detail and depth of understanding, though this perception of complete understanding can be illusory.
concepts.content: Visual perception cannot be formulated as a simple input-output function over predefined domains. Vision is a dynamical system, even when looking at a static image. The longer you look at an image, the more details you see and the better you understand the scene. (see figure: A street in Paris. Is everything fine in this picture?) But this feeling of unlimited and effortless understanding of a picture is also an illusion. For instance, while a viewer might feel they understand everything they see, they may fail to make sense of all the chair legs in @fig-street_in_paris, as the image has been manipulated so that some legs do not correspond to any chair.
concepts.motivation_md: Treating vision as a dynamical process acknowledges that scene understanding is an active, time-dependent exploration rather than an instantaneous computation.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is a dynamical process where understanding deepens over time.

concepts.one_liner: Visual cognitive load describes the phenomenon where an increase in the mental demand of a visual task makes judgment mistakes more likely.
concepts.content: When solving a task, as the **visual cognitive load** increases, we are more likely to make judgment mistakes.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept helps explain human and system performance limits in complex visual tasks, highlighting how complexity impacts accuracy.
concepts.recap_md: - Increased visual cognitive load correlates with a higher frequency of errors.

concepts.title: Images as datasets of patches

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: Large images can be viewed as datasets of thousands of tiny image patches, allowing techniques designed for big data to be applied to individual photos.
concepts.content: As you look around an image, notice that each patch you look at is actually a small photo in its own right. In fact, a large image contains thousands of tiny images within it. A single photo can be considered "big data"; if you chop up this photo, you get a big dataset of tiny images. A common trick in computer vision is to take a method that was developed for processing a dataset and instead apply it to the set of patches in an image, or vice versa. ![Each picture contains lots of images.](figures/visionscience/tiny_images.jpg){#fig-tiny_images width="100%"}
concepts.motivation_md: Conceptualizing images as collections of patches allows researchers to leverage powerful statistical and machine learning tools originally designed for large-scale datasets.
concepts.recap_md: - A single image can be decomposed into a large dataset of small patches.

concepts.title: Applying dataset methods to image patches

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: A common computer vision technique involves applying methods developed for large datasets to the individual patches within a single image, or vice versa.
concepts.content: A common trick in computer vision is to take a method that was developed for processing a dataset and instead apply it to the set of patches in an image, or vice versa. This allows for the repurposing of dataset-level algorithms for local image analysis.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique enables the use of robust statistical models on a single image by treating its internal structure as a population of samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Dataset-level methods can be applied to the collection of patches within one image.

concepts.title: The eye of the artist
concepts.one_liner: Learning to paint teaches one to see the world not just as objects, but as a series of light, shadows, and strokes that create the illusion of reality.
concepts.content: Learning to paint is a great way of learning to see. Starting from a white canvas and a finite set of acrylic paints, the goal is to paint an object that looks real, with shadows, 3D shape, and reflections. Artists learn to see the world not by what it represents, but by why it looks the way it does. The following sequence @fig-agata_painting, painted by Agata Lapedriza, shows different steps in the painting process of a strawberry. Layer after layer, the artist replicates the light that will fool your eye into seeing a strawberry instead of acrylic paint. It is interesting to see that the realism does not increase monotonically as the painting progresses; for instance, from step 3 to 4, the right side of the strawberry has lost realism, but those new strokes will become the shading that makes the strawberry pop out from the canvas. ![The following sequence shows different steps in the process of painting a strawberry. Source: Original images by Agata Lapedriza.](figures/visionscience/strawberries.png){#fig-agata_painting}
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the artistic process provides insight into how visual cues like shading and highlights are constructed to create the perception of three-dimensional form.
concepts.recap_md: - Painting requires understanding the underlying reasons for an object's appearance.

prereq.rationale: This technique is the direct application of the conceptual framework that treats a single image as a dataset of patches.
Motion blur is a temporal artifact of the image formation process, which is fundamentally based on the camera models like the pinhole.

overlay.rationale: Cognitive load is a factor that influences the accuracy and limits of the dynamical process of visual perception.
Both concepts deal with the relationship between local image components (patches or pixels) and their broader context.
Motion blur provides a concrete example of how vision must account for temporal dynamics and movement rather than just static snapshots.
Unlike a standard pinhole camera that captures a single projection, light field cameras capture a dense array of views simultaneously.
The definition of a pinhole camera provides the formal optical mechanism for the natural image formation observed in tree shadows.
The definition of vanishing points and the horizon line provides the formal geometric basis for the perception of horizontal and vertical surfaces.
